title: Follow Jesus through Jericho, where Zacchaeus climbed a tree
note: Markers show approximate areas. The line to Jerusalem is illustrative, not a surveyed road. Modern borders are shown only for orientation.

jericho.name: Jericho
jericho.text: In the first century the town centered south of the old mound, near the mouth of Wadi Qelt, where Herod the Great built winter palaces at a site now called Tulul Abu el-Alayiq. Luke does not say where in Jericho the sycamore-fig stood or where Zacchaeus lived (Luke 19:1–5).

tell.name: Tell es-Sultan
tell.text: The ancient mound beside the spring of Ein es-Sultan, the Jericho of Joshua 6. By Jesus' day it was an old ruin, and the town had moved south. Tradition links the spring with Elisha's healing of Jericho's water (2 Kings 2:19–22).

bethany.name: Bethany
bethany.text: Usually identified with the village of al-Eizariya on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives. Luke says Jesus approached Bethphage and Bethany after leaving Jericho, on the last stretch of the road to Jerusalem (Luke 19:29).

jerusalem.name: Jerusalem
jerusalem.text: Luke frames the Jericho visit as part of Jesus' final journey up to Jerusalem (Luke 19:11, 28). The city stood high in the Judean hills, far above the Jordan Valley.

chapters.title: An oasis below sea level
chapters.html:
Luke says Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through on his way up to Jerusalem. Just before, a blind man by the roadside near the town had called out to him and received his sight.

Jericho was a spring-fed oasis in the Jordan Valley, ringed by desert. In Jesus' day the town lay south of the ancient mound of Joshua's time, near the palaces Herod the Great had built. Its palm groves and balsam made it wealthy.
facts: Jericho is often called the lowest city on earth, at roughly 850 feet (about 258 m) below sea level.
The Old Testament calls Jericho the City of Palms (Deuteronomy 34:3), and the historian Josephus praised its date palms and balsam. Josephus also reports that Herod the Great died at Jericho.

chapters.title: A short man in a sycamore-fig
chapters.html:
Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector, and he was wealthy. Jericho's valuable produce and its position near the fords of the Jordan made it a natural place to collect taxes and tolls.

He wanted to see who Jesus was, but he was short and the crowd blocked his view. So he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore-fig tree along the route Jesus was about to take.
facts: The sycamore-fig (Ficus sycomorus) is a kind of fig, not the sycamore of North America or Europe. Its short trunk and low, spreading branches make it easy to climb. The prophet Amos also tended these trees (Amos 7:14).
The name Zacchaeus is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Zakkai (Ezra 2:9), usually understood to mean pure or innocent.

chapters.title: Salvation comes to this house
chapters.html:
When Jesus reached the spot, he looked up, called Zacchaeus by name and told him he must stay at his house today. Zacchaeus came down at once and welcomed him gladly, while the crowd muttered that Jesus had gone to be the guest of a sinner.

Zacchaeus promised to give half his possessions to the poor and to repay four times over anyone he had cheated. Jesus said that salvation had come to this house, because Zacchaeus too was a son of Abraham.
quote: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.
facts: The Law of Moses required a thief to repay four sheep for one stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1). For other wrongs it required repayment plus a fifth (Numbers 5:6–7). Zacchaeus chose the stricter measure.
Luke places this story soon after a rich ruler became very sad when Jesus told him to sell everything and give to the poor (Luke 18:18–25).

chapters.title: Going up to Jerusalem
chapters.html:
Because Jesus was near Jerusalem and people expected God's kingdom to appear at once, he told the parable of the ten minas. Then he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.

The road from Jericho climbs steeply through the Judean Wilderness to Bethphage and Bethany on the Mount of Olives. From there Jesus sent two disciples ahead to bring a colt for his entry into the city.
facts: The climb from Jericho to the Mount of Olives rises roughly 3,300 feet (about 1,000 m), which is why travelers spoke of going up to Jerusalem.
Jesus set the parable of the good Samaritan on this same road, with a man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10:30).
